parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones to book a table and a cake for a birthday dinner at a restaurant.
script: Good afternoon, The Olive Tree restaurant.
Hi, I'd like to book a table for a birthday dinner, please.
We'll be eleven. Oh, wait, my cousin can't come now. So ten.
Ten people on Friday the 19th. What time would you like?
Seven thirty is fully booked, I'm afraid, for a group that size. We could do seven, or eight fifteen.
Seven is better. Some of us have children.
Seven o'clock, then. Would you like to sit in the main room or in our private room upstairs?
The private room sounds nice. Is there an extra charge?
There's no charge for the room itself, but groups of eight or more need to choose from our set menu, which is 32 pounds per person for three courses.
That's fine. Do you have vegetarian options?
Yes, there are vegetarian and vegan options on the set menu. If anyone has an allergy, just let us know in advance.
One of the children is allergic to nuts.
I'll make a note. Is the birthday for one of the adults?
Yes, my mother. She's turning seventy. Could you make a cake?
Our chef can make one. Chocolate or lemon?
Lemon, please. She doesn't like chocolate.
Lemon. And would you like a message on it?
Lovely. The cake is 25 pounds, and we'll need a deposit of 50 pounds to hold the room. Can I take a name?
Thank you, Ms Nasser. We'll send you a confirmation by text.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide speaks to visitors at the start of a tour of a chocolate factory.
script: Welcome to the Brightwater Chocolate Factory. I'm Dana, and I'll be your guide for the next hour and a half.

The factory was founded in 1902 by two sisters, Edith and May Brightwater, who started by making chocolate in their kitchen. Today we produce around twenty tonnes of chocolate a day, but we still use Edith's original recipe for our plain chocolate.

Before we start, some important rules. For hygiene reasons, everyone must wear a hairnet and a white coat in the production areas. You'll find these at the cloakroom. Photos are allowed in most areas, but not in the recipe room, for obvious reasons. And please don't touch any of the machines.
One thing visitors often ask: can we eat the chocolate? Yes, you'll have the chance to taste chocolate at three points during the tour, and at the end you'll each receive a small box to take home.

The tour finishes in the shop, where everything is twenty per cent cheaper than in supermarkets. The shop also sells broken pieces from the production line very cheaply, which are popular with bakers.

Let me explain the route. We begin here in the entrance hall. From here we walk to the history room, which is the first door on the left, where you can see the sisters' original equipment. Then we go upstairs to the viewing gallery, which looks down on the main production floor. At the end of the gallery is the tasting room, where you'll try chocolates from different countries.
After that we come back downstairs to the packing area, which is opposite the history room. And finally, at the back of the building, next to the car park exit, is the shop and café.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two apprentices, Sam and Leila, discuss their electrical engineering course with their trainer.
script: So, you're both halfway through the first year of the apprenticeship. How's it going?
Mostly good. The practical work on site is the best part. I find the college days harder, especially the maths.
For me it's the opposite. I like the theory, but I was nervous on site at first. Everyone was much more experienced.
That's very normal. Leila, has that improved?
Yes. My supervisor let me shadow her for two weeks before I did anything on my own. That really helped.
Good. Now, Sam, about the maths. There's a free support session on Wednesday afternoons at the college. Have you tried it?
Not yet. I didn't know it existed.
I'd strongly recommend it. Many apprentices find it makes a big difference before the exams.
The written exam is in June. The practical assessment is earlier, in April, so that you have time to retake it if necessary.
What does the practical assessment involve?

You'll wire a small domestic installation, a kitchen circuit, and then test it. You'll have four hours. The most common reason people fail is not the wiring itself but the testing and the paperwork, so practise those.
Can we use our own tools?
Yes, but they'll be checked for safety first. Make sure they're in good condition.
One more thing. Do we get paid for college days?
Yes, college days count as working days, so you're paid as normal. But if you miss a college day without a good reason, it's treated as an unpaid absence.
Most apprentices are offered a permanent job by their employer. Some go on to specialise, for example in solar installations or electric vehicle charging, which are growing fast.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A talk about noise pollution and health.
script: When we think about pollution, we usually think about the air or water. But noise is also a serious environmental problem, and one that is often ignored.
The World Health Organization considers noise the second most harmful environmental factor in Europe, after air pollution. The main source is road traffic, followed by railways and aircraft.

How does noise affect health? The most obvious effect is on sleep. Even when people do not wake up, noise at night can raise the heart rate and blood pressure. Over many years, this is linked to a higher risk of heart disease.

Noise also affects children's learning. A well-known study compared schools near a busy airport with similar schools in quieter areas. Children at the noisy schools had poorer reading skills and memory, and the effect was greatest in schools directly under the flight path.
Interestingly, people do not get used to noise as much as they think. Many say they no longer notice it, but measurements show that their bodies still react.

What can be done? Some solutions are technical. Quieter road surfaces can reduce traffic noise by several decibels, and noise barriers beside motorways are now common. Electric vehicles are much quieter at low speeds, although at higher speeds most of the noise comes from the tyres rather than the engine.

Other solutions involve planning. Placing bedrooms on the quiet side of a building, away from the road, can make a large difference. And green spaces help too: not because trees block much sound, but because people who have access to a quiet park report less stress from noise at home.
Finally, some cities now produce noise maps, showing noise levels street by street. These maps help planners decide where to build homes, schools and hospitals.

paras: A  QuickShift. Same-day moves available if you call before 10 am. Prices from £180 for a one-bedroom flat. Packing boxes are sold separately.
B  Careful Hands. Specialists in moving pianos, antiques and artwork. Every item is insured up to £50,000. Free home visit to give a quote.

passages.title: Coastline Care Homes: induction for new care assistants
paras: During your first two weeks, you will work alongside an experienced care assistant and will not be counted in the staffing numbers. This gives you time to learn routines and get to know residents.

You must complete the Care Certificate within twelve weeks of starting. It covers fifteen standards, including communication, dignity, safeguarding and basic life support. Study is done partly online and partly through observed practice.
Before working alone with residents, you need a clear background check. Your manager will tell you when this has been received.
Each resident has a care plan describing their needs and preferences. Read the care plan of every resident you support, and record any changes you notice in the daily log.
Never give medication unless you have completed the medication training and been assessed as competent.
Supervision meetings with your line manager take place every six weeks. These are a chance to discuss your progress and any concerns.

passages.title: Saving energy in the office
paras: A  Computers left on overnight waste a surprising amount of electricity. Switch them off at the end of the day, along with monitors and printers. Set screens to sleep after five minutes without use.
B  Heating is the largest energy cost in most offices. Keep windows closed when the heating is on, and if the office is too warm, turn down the thermostat rather than opening a window.
C  Make use of daylight. Open blinds in the morning, and switch off lights in meeting rooms and toilets when they are not in use. Motion sensors are being fitted in all corridors this year.
D  The kitchen uses more energy than you might think. Boil only the amount of water you need, and do not leave the dishwasher running half empty.
E  Think about travel. Video calls can often replace short business trips, and staff who cycle to work can use the new showers on the ground floor.
F  Each department has an energy champion who collects ideas from colleagues. The best suggestion each quarter wins a day's extra holiday.

passages.title: The science of queuing
paras: A  Waiting in line is one of the most common experiences of modern life. It has been estimated that the average person in a developed country spends several months of their life in queues: at supermarkets, airports, banks and on the phone. Yet the frustration we feel depends less on how long we actually wait than on how the wait feels.

B  This idea was explored in a famous paper by David Maister in 1985, which set out a number of principles of waiting. Among them: unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time; uncertain waits feel longer than known, finite waits; and unfair waits feel longer than equitable ones. Businesses have used these principles ever since.

C  A frequently told story concerns an airport in Houston, where passengers complained about waiting for their luggage. The airport hired more staff, reducing the wait to eight minutes, but complaints continued. The problem was that passengers walked for only one minute from the plane and then stood at the carousel for seven. The airport moved the arrival gates further away, so that passengers walked for six minutes and waited for two. Complaints almost disappeared.

D  Fairness matters too. Many shops have replaced several separate lines with a single 'serpentine' queue that feeds all the checkouts. On average, this does not reduce waiting time, but it removes the annoying experience of watching the next line move faster than yours. Customers report higher satisfaction, even when their wait is slightly longer.

E  Information can also transform the experience. Theme parks display estimated waiting times at the start of each line, and these are often deliberately set slightly longer than the real wait, so that visitors are pleasantly surprised. Telephone systems that announce a caller's position in the queue reduce the number of people who hang up.

F  Cultural expectations play a part as well. In some countries, orderly queuing is regarded as a basic social rule, and people who push in face strong disapproval. In others, getting served depends more on attracting attention. Researchers caution, however, that national stereotypes about queuing are often exaggerated, and that behaviour depends heavily on the situation.
